newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African truth probe calls up former minister.
newsitem.headline: S.African truth probe calls up former minister.

text.p: Former police minister Adriaan Vlok will become the first member of an apartheid-era cabinet to be forced to testify to South Africa's truth commission on human rights crimes, officials said on Thursday.

Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, trying to clear up and heal the country's murky past, will on Friday subpoena Vlok and eight former police generals to appear at closed hearings of the body.
Tutu's deputy, Alex Boraine, told a news conference that Vlok and the others would be asked to tell all they know about human rights violations under apartheid.

In what he called a breakthrough for the probe into the human rights record of white rule, Boraine said in an interview later that five unidentified police officers had applied to the commission for amnesty.

"I think this is the breakthrough we have been waiting for. These five senior policemen have already given us information on what happened in cases that have baffled our police and courts for many years.
"They are prepared to give details of gross human rights violations and they are prepared to name names," he told Reuters.
Boraine said the commission decided to subpoena the officers when they failed to submit satisfactory written evidence on the actions of police under white rule.
"The subpoenas are ready. The process will start on Friday -- it will be a matter of finding the people."
He said Vlok's name was added to the list because he had been named at a number of the commission's public hearings for victms of human rights abuses.
"We will be asking him a number of questions about the allegations that have been made," Boraine said.

Vlok was in charge of the police at the height of emergency rule in the mid 1980s, when hundreds of black activists were killed by police and up to 30,000 people were detained without charge amid countless allegations of torture in prisons.

The white-led National Party, which ruled South Africa for nearly five decades and implemented apartheid, reacted to the announcement saying the action against Vlok would be in conflict with a procedural understanding it had with the commission.

"At this stage it would create serious problems if the commission were to subpoena Mr Vlok or any members of the previous government with a view to giving evidence of a general nature on a wide spectrum of issues," a party statement said.

Boraine said former police commissioners Johan van der Merwe, Mike Geldenhuys, Johan Coetzee and Hennie de Witt as well as senior generals Basie Smit, Johan le Roux, Krappies Engelbrecht and Bertus Steyn would now be summoned.
It will be up to the commission to decide whether to go public with their testimony after the closed hearings. More former policemen will be subpoenaed later, he added.
"We hope that our actions and the applications by the five police officers will encourage many others to come forward. We hope this will be the trickle that becomes a flood," Boraine said.
